scenes.heading: Circuit Breakers & Resilience
scenes.narration: Let's take a minute on circuit breakers, the pattern that stops one slow dependency from taking down your whole system.

scenes.heading: Why a breaker exists
items: A sick dependency plus retries causes cascading failure
The breaker trips open and fails fast instead of hammering it
Failing fast bounds latency and frees goroutines
scenes.narration: When a downstream dependency slows down or starts failing, the worst thing your service can do is keep calling and keep retrying. Those calls pile up, exhaust connection pools and goroutines, and your service goes down too, a cascading failure. A circuit breaker borrows from electrical engineering: it watches the failure rate and, once failures cross a threshold, it trips open and fails fast for a cooldown, giving the sick dependency room to recover.

scenes.heading: The three states
steps: Closed: calls flow, outcomes are counted
Threshold crossed on a failure ratio -> Open
Open: fail fast instantly for a cooldown
scenes.narration: A breaker is a finite state machine. In Closed, requests flow and every outcome updates counters in a rolling window. When the failure ratio crosses the threshold over enough requests, it records the time and moves to Open, rejecting calls instantly for a cooldown. After the cooldown it goes Half-Open and admits a few probe calls. If the probes succeed it returns to Closed; a single failure re-opens it and restarts the cooldown.

scenes.heading: sony/gobreaker in practice
scenes.narration: gobreaker is the de-facto Go library. Here ReadyToTrip opens the breaker only when failures exceed fifty percent over at least twenty requests, so a low-traffic blip doesn't trip it but a real meltdown does. Execute runs the protected call and records the outcome. When the breaker is open, Execute returns ErrOpenState instantly without touching the dependency, and we serve a cached fallback instead.

scenes.text: A breaker rarely works alone: combine timeouts, jittered backoff retries, a bulkhead, and a fallback for end-to-end resilience.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: a breaker is one layer, not a whole solution. Time out each attempt with context, retry transient failures with exponential backoff plus jitter so clients don't synchronize, bound concurrency with a bulkhead so one slow dependency can't exhaust all goroutines, and always have a fallback for when the breaker is open. Composed together, these turn a total outage into a merely degraded feature.
